items.explanation: The passage stresses that Puritans treated wealth as a trust from God with duties and responsibilities, and that statute books and court records are full of government-set price and wage controls. Because communal fairness norms — the medieval moral economy of just price and just wage — governed economic life, magistrates acted on them even without a specific authorizing statute.
options: (A) Wealth was a trust from God carrying communal obligations, so norms of a 'just price' and 'just wage' could override the absence of written law.
(B) Puritan courts held that magistrates could invent new laws whenever the colony's treasury ran short of funds.
(C) The General Court believed wealthy merchants were secretly working as agents of the Anglican hierarchy.
(D) Puritans held that English common law automatically permitted any penalty a magistrate chose to impose.
items.stem: What underlying Puritan belief made it possible for magistrates to fine the merchant in 1639 even though no statute authorized the penalty?
items.stimulus: Although some Puritan values resembled the rising capitalist ethic, Puritan economic life remained closer to the medieval than the modern. Unrestrained economic individualism would have alarmed any respectable Puritan. The statute books and court records of seventeenth-century Massachusetts are full of government-set price and wage controls. Puritans treated wealth as a trust from God, stressing duties and responsibilities alongside the benefits of work and gain. In 1639 the colony's General Court fined one of its richest merchants for excessive profiteering — though no statute prohibited the practice. The Puritans never separated religion from business and kept repeating the medieval idea of the 'just price.' Over the long run, though, once the Puritan work ethic was divorced from its religious setting, it quickened the spirit of capitalism: the old restraints on the individual gradually gave way to the enterprising, self-made figure who rose by his own exertions. — adapted from Gerald N. Grob and Robert N. Beck, American Ideas (1963)

option_explanations.A: Correct. The passage describes a Puritan moral economy: wealth was a trust from God, carrying duties and responsibilities alongside the benefits of gain, and the statute books and court records of seventeenth-century Massachusetts are full of government-set price and wage controls. Under that belief, the communal norms of a 'just price' and a 'just wage' had real authority — enough that magistrates could enforce them in 1639 even when no written statute authorized the particular penalty. The fine rested on the shared religious duty of economic fairness, not on a statute.
option_explanations.B: This invents a motive the passage never mentions. Nothing in the passage suggests magistrates fined merchants to raise revenue or that they believed they could invent laws whenever the treasury was short. Their intervention came from the moral duty to enforce a just price — a communal religious obligation — not fiscal opportunism.
option_explanations.C: The passage contains no evidence of an Anglican-conspiracy theory behind the fine. The merchant was penalized for violating economic fairness norms, not suspected of spying for the Church of England. This option confuses Puritan hostility to the Anglican hierarchy with the actual basis of the penalty described.
option_explanations.D: This misstates the legal basis of the fine. The Puritans did not believe English common law gave magistrates a blank check to impose any penalty they wished. The point of the passage is precisely the opposite: it was the shared moral-religious norm of the 'just price' — not any formal law, common or statutory — that made the fine legitimate in Puritan eyes.

items.explanation: The passage's thesis is the paradox: Puritan asceticism and the 'calling' bred hard work and wealth, and as strict religious orthodoxy faded, those work habits fused with market freedom — producing a market-oriented economy out of a moral one.
options: (A) Puritan limits on trade kept New England's economy permanently behind the southern and middle colonies.
(B) New England under the Puritans reproduced the feudal manor system of medieval Europe, with estates passing from father to son over generations.
(C) As Puritan orthodoxy faded, Puritan work habits fused with freer markets into a market economy.
(D) New England's economy began to grow only after non-Puritan immigrants arrived in large numbers after 1640.
items.stem: Which statement best captures the main argument the authors make in the passage?

option_explanations.A: The passage never claims New England was permanently behind the other regions. Its argument is developmental: the same moral economy that initially restrained markets later transformed into one. A claim about permanent regional inferiority contradicts the passage's thesis of growth.
option_explanations.B: This confuses two different meanings of 'medieval.' The passage says Puritan economic life resembled the medieval moral economy — norms of just price and communal obligation — not that New England reproduced the feudal manor system. Puritan landholding was based on freehold family farms, not manorial estates with hereditary lordship.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The passage's central paradox is that Puritan asceticism and the doctrine of the 'calling' bred disciplined, hard-working producers who accumulated wealth; then, as strict religious orthodoxy faded in the later 1600s, those ingrained work habits fused with freer market conditions. The result was a market-oriented economy that grew out of a moral one — the Puritan work ethic surviving its original religious container.
option_explanations.D: The passage does not credit non-Puritan immigration after 1640 with starting growth. The economic transformation it describes was internal: Puritan work habits persisting and adapting as orthodoxy weakened, not an outside population arriving to build the economy. (In fact, large-scale non-Puritan immigration to New England came much later.)

items.explanation: When asked what drove the rebels, Josephe answered with the concrete abuses they suffered: Spanish officials beat them, seized their property, and forced them to work without pay. The revolt was a response to these material exploitations of the colonial labor and tribute system, not to trade, foreign aid, or internal succession politics.
options: (A) A dispute among Pueblo leaders over who would govern once the Spanish were expelled.
(B) A desire to reopen the pre-contact trade routes that Spanish missions had closed off.
(C) Promises of military aid from English colonists on the Atlantic coast.
(D) Specific daily abuses of colonial rule: beatings, seizure of their property, and forced labor without pay.
items.stem: Josephe's testimony indicates that the Pueblo rebels' motives centered most directly on which of the following?
items.stimulus: Asked what drove the rebels to renounce Spanish authority, Josephe — a Spanish-speaking Pueblo Indian questioned by colonial officials after the 1680 uprising — answered that the causes were the ill treatment they suffered: Spanish officials beat them, seized their property, and forced them to work without pay. Asked why the rebels burned churches and images, mocked sacred objects, and killed priests, Josephe said he had heard it stated that while besieging the Spanish villa the rebels shouted that the Spaniards' God was dead and that only their own gods lived. Their captains ordered that the names of Jesus and Mary never be spoken, and Josephe reported seeing new houses of native worship built where the people danced their traditional ceremonial dances. — paraphrased from the 1681 interrogation of Josephe

option_explanations.A: Josephe says nothing about a succession dispute among Pueblo leaders. When asked what drove the rebels to renounce Spanish authority, he points to the treatment the Pueblo suffered — beatings, seized property, unpaid forced labor — not to a power struggle over who would govern afterward.
option_explanations.B: Trade routes appear nowhere in Josephe's testimony. His answer to the 'why' question is entirely about abuse under colonial rule. This option substitutes a plausible-sounding motive for the one the witness actually named.
option_explanations.C: Historically implausible and absent from the testimony. The Pueblo peoples of New Mexico had no contact with English colonists on the Atlantic coast, who were over a thousand miles away and preoccupied with their own colonies. Josephe never mentions English aid; the revolt was a Pueblo-led action driven by local grievances.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Josephe answered the question about the rebels' motives directly and concretely: Spanish officials beat them, seized their property, and forced them to work without pay. The revolt's center was the material exploitation of the colonial labor and tribute system — specific daily abuses of Spanish rule — not foreign aid, trade, or internal politics.

items.explanation: The rebels burned churches, banned the names of Jesus and Mary, and rebuilt native ceremonial houses — attacking the religious-cultural apparatus of colonization alongside the labor/tribute system, i.e., a bid for cultural and political autonomy, not just economic redress.
options: (A) The rebels had been so thoroughly Christianized that their uprising was purely an economic protest.
(B) The rebels limited themselves to peaceful, nonviolent forms of protest against Spanish rule.
(C) The rebels attacked Spanish religious and cultural symbols as well as the colonial labor system.
(D) The rebels traded freely with the Spanish and rebelled only against new taxes on that trade.
items.stem: Josephe's testimony indicates that the Pueblo rebels did which of the following?

option_explanations.A: The testimony shows the opposite: far from being thoroughly Christianized, the rebels renounced Christianity — burning churches and images, banning the names of Jesus and Mary, and rebuilding native ceremonial houses. And the uprising was not purely economic, since these acts targeted the religious and cultural apparatus of colonization, not just labor conditions.
option_explanations.B: This contradicts the testimony's facts. The rebels besieged the Spanish villa, killed priests, and burned churches and sacred objects — a violent uprising, not peaceful nonviolent protest.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Josephe's testimony shows the rebellion had two targets. The rebels burned churches, mocked sacred objects, banned the names of Jesus and Mary, and rebuilt native ceremonial houses — an attack on Spanish religious and cultural symbols — while also rebelling against the colonial labor system of beatings, tribute, and forced work. It was a bid for cultural and political autonomy, not merely an economic grievance.
option_explanations.D: The testimony describes no free trade and no tax revolt. The Pueblo did not trade freely with the Spanish — they labored under the encomienda/repartimiento system — and Josephe's listed grievances are beatings, seizure of property, and unpaid forced labor, not new taxes on commerce.

items.explanation: After retaking New Mexico in the 1690s, Spanish authorities shifted policy: they appointed an official to defend Pueblo rights, tolerated some native religious practices, and relied more on missionary persuasion — a limited accommodation, distinct from the Anglo pattern of removal.
options: (A) Spanish authorities accommodated certain aspects of Pueblo culture in the late 1600s and 1700s.
(B) Spanish armies and disease completely eliminated the Pueblo population of the Southwest.
(C) Defeated by the rebels, Spain permanently abandoned all its territorial claims in North America by 1700.
(D) Spain and Britain allied to impose joint European control over the interior of North America.
items.stem: Which of the following best describes Spanish policy in the region in the decades after the events Josephe describes?

option_explanations.A: Correct. After the 1680 revolt, Spain could not reconquer New Mexico until the 1690s, and the reconquest was followed by a deliberate policy shift. Spanish authorities appointed an official to defend Pueblo rights, tolerated some native religious practices rather than forcing conversion, and relied more on missionary persuasion than coercion — a limited accommodation of Pueblo culture that contrasted with the Anglo pattern of removal. The lesson of 1680 was that the old severity was unsustainable.
option_explanations.B: Historically false. The Pueblo peoples were not eliminated; their communities survived the revolt, the reconquest, and the entire colonial period — many Pueblo towns exist to this day. The revolt drove the Spanish out for twelve years, not the Pueblo out of existence.
option_explanations.C: This gets the chronology of empire backward. Spain did not abandon North America — it reconquered New Mexico in the 1690s and held its southwestern borderlands (New Mexico, Texas, Florida) into the nineteenth century. The 1680 revolt was a temporary, regional expulsion, not an imperial withdrawal.
option_explanations.D: Spain and Britain were imperial rivals, not partners, throughout the colonial period — they fought each other repeatedly from the 1500s through the 1700s. There was no joint Anglo-Spanish administration of North America's interior; the two empires contested the continent against each other.
